title: Beyond linear regression: logistic regression and an overview of models

videos.script: Every regression so far predicted a number: minutes, reais, orders. Many of the questions Horta cares about have a yes-or-no answer instead. Will this customer complain? Will this delivery be late? Will this visitor buy? {{yesno}} A straight line is the wrong tool for those. Fit one to zeros and ones and it happily predicts a complaint probability below zero for a quick delivery, and above one for a slow one. {{wrong}} Logistic regression fixes that by fitting an S-shaped curve that stays between zero and one. Underneath, it is still a straight line, but on a different scale: the log of the odds. {{scale}} Its coefficients become odds ratios. A first-time customer's odds of complaining are about two and a half times a returning customer's, at the same delivery time. {{ratio}} Then the probabilities become decisions, such as which orders to follow up with a phone call. Every such decision trades catching more real complaints against raising more false alarms. {{tradeoff}} The lesson ends with a map: which kind of model fits which kind of outcome, and where the machine-learning course takes over. {{map}}
